title: Northwind AI x Redwood — Technical deep dive: SDK retries + streaming reliability
summary: Northwind AI raised concerns about client-side retry storms during 429/5xx events and about streaming disconnects (especially behind corporate proxies / L7 gateways). Redwood walked through current API behavior (Retry-After, request_id), recommended retry guidance (exponential backoff + jitter, max attempts, honoring Retry-After), and why streaming retries are intentionally conservative to avoid duplicate side effects. Redwood SE referenced an upcoming cross-language SDK standardization effort (Python/TypeScript/Go) to align auth precedence, typed errors, retry/backoff defaults, timeout model, and streaming semantics, plus a conformance test suite.
topics: Retry storms / thundering herd risk and safe client defaults
Which status codes and network errors are retryable
Streaming disconnect failure modes behind proxies
Partial output, request_id propagation, and debugging
Idempotency guidance and duplicate billing concerns
next_steps: Redwood to share draft SDK retry/timeout standard + proposed defaults (incl. Retry-After + jitter) with Northwind for review.
Northwind to send a few anonymized logs showing streaming disconnect patterns (proxy vendor, idle timeouts, and whether FIN/RST).
Redwood to provide a minimal repro example in Python + TypeScript demonstrating recommended streaming cancellation + retry handling.
Schedule a follow-up (30 min) after Northwind tests a beta SDK build / branch once available.
action_items: Ibrahim Khan — Send Northwind the SDK standardization overview + retry/timeout guidance doc links — Due 2026-01-26
Samira El-Amin — Share proxy/gateway details and disconnect logs (timestamps + request_id if available) — Due 2026-01-30
Jared Kim — Provide Northwind’s current retry config (max attempts, backoff, which errors) for comparison — Due 2026-01-30
Monica Patel — Coordinate follow-up meeting and include SRE stakeholder if needed — Due 2026-01-27
transcript:
Meeting Header
Date: Jan 23, 2026
Time: 10:02 AM PST
Duration: 56 minutes
Organizer: Monica Patel (Redwood Inference)
Attendees (Redwood): Monica Patel, Ibrahim Khan
Attendees (Northwind AI): Samira El-Amin, Jared Kim, Priya Nair

Auto Summary (Fireflies)
- Customer asked how Redwood avoids retry storms when 429s spike.
- Customer reported streaming responses sometimes disconnect mid-generation behind a corporate proxy.
- Redwood explained recommended retry defaults (exponential backoff w/ jitter, respect Retry-After, limited attempts) and why streaming retries are not automatic.
- Redwood mentioned upcoming work to standardize retries/timeouts/streaming across Python/TS/Go SDKs.


[00:00] Monica Patel: Cool. Okay, I think we’re live. Thanks everyone for making time. This is more of a technical deep dive, so Ibrahim is here, he leads a lot of the SDK behavior stuff.

[00:12] Samira El-Amin: Great, thanks. Yeah we wanted to go deeper than the doc page. We had a couple incidents with other providers where the SDK basically DOS’d the endpoint when rate limits hit.

[00:24] Ibrahim Khan: Yep. Totally fair. And just to level set, what language are you guys primarily calling from today?

[00:29] Priya Nair: TypeScript in production, but we have some Python batch jobs too.

[00:34] Jared Kim: And I’m the one that gets paged when the retry loop goes sideways.

[00:38] Monica Patel: (laughs) Yeah, we want to avoid that.

[00:41] Ibrahim Khan: So two big buckets: (1) retries/backoff/timeout defaults and how we classify errors, and (2) streaming semantics. Samira, you mentioned retry storms and streaming disconnects. Which is more painful right now?

[00:55] Samira El-Amin: Retry storms. We saw 429s, then the client retried fast, then we got more 429s. It became a feedback loop.

[01:05] Jared Kim: And the biggest issue is it was not consistent. Like TS did one thing, Python did another with the same settings.

[01:13] Ibrahim Khan: Yeah. That last point is… you’re not wrong. We’re actually in the middle of standardizing behavior across the SDKs specifically because of “works in TS but not in Python” type issues.

[01:24] Monica Patel: That’s one of the reasons we’re doing this call now, to give you the plan and the current best practice.

[01:31] Samira El-Amin: Okay, so concretely. When you return 429, do you always send Retry-After?

[01:38] Ibrahim Khan: The gateway is moving to “always” for 429. Historically it was… mostly, but not perfectly consistent depending on which edge path you hit. The platform team has a fix in flight to consistently emit Retry-After on 429. When it’s present, our SDK policy is to honor it.

[01:58] Jared Kim: Honor it meaning, no backoff calc, just sleep for that duration?

[02:03] Ibrahim Khan: Prefer Retry-After if it’s sane and within bounds. Otherwise fallback to exponential backoff with jitter. And we cap it, because we don’t want a single request sleeping for like two hours.

[02:14] Priya Nair: What’s “sane”?

[02:16] Ibrahim Khan: Usually “seconds” format or an HTTP date. If it parses and it’s not negative. We also clamp to a max backoff.

[02:26] Samira El-Amin: What are your default attempts? Because some SDKs do like 10 and that’s too much for us.

[02:33] Ibrahim Khan: We’re aligning on a conservative default. Today it’s inconsistent across languages, which is exactly what we’re fixing. The upcoming standard is: limited attempts, exponential backoff with jitter, and only for retryable classes: 429, and a set of 5xx, plus network-ish errors like connect reset/timeouts.

[02:55] Jared Kim: Which 5xx? All of them?

[02:58] Ibrahim Khan: Not all. Like 501 isn’t really helpful to retry. The general default is: 500, 502, 503, 504. And 429. Plus network errors where you didn’t get a response.

[03:12] Samira El-Amin: Do you retry 408?

[03:14] Ibrahim Khan: That’s one of those “depends” codes. Some stacks treat 408 as retryable. We generally consider timeouts at the client layer (connect/read/overall), and if the server sends 408 we can treat it as retryable, but we’re cautious because 408 can be from a proxy.

[03:30] Monica Patel: Also, for billing concerns, we try to avoid retries on 4xx other than 429.

[03:36] Priya Nair: We had a provider retry on 400 once. It was a nightmare.

[03:40] Ibrahim Khan: Yeah, we won’t do that. If a client retries a 400, that’s a bug. Part of our standardization is a typed error taxonomy where “retryable” is explicit.

[03:53] Jared Kim: Okay but the storm question: even if you backoff, if 1,000 clients all backoff the same way you still herd.

[04:00] Ibrahim Khan: Exactly. That’s why jitter matters. Without jitter, everyone retries at 1s, 2s, 4s, etc. With jitter it spreads. We use exponential backoff plus randomization.

[04:12] Samira El-Amin: Full jitter or equal jitter? Like AWS style?

[04:16] Ibrahim Khan: We’re leaning toward full jitter for 429 to reduce synchronization, with guardrails. The SRE team has strong opinions here because of load impact.

[04:27] Jared Kim: So you’ve actually measured it?

[04:29] Monica Patel: Yes, our SRE folks ran impact analysis. The big takeaway was: keep max attempts modest, honor Retry-After, add jitter, and don’t retry on non-retryable stuff.

[04:42] Priya Nair: Can we configure it? Because we might want different behavior for batch vs user-facing.

[04:47] Ibrahim Khan: Yes. Configurable max attempts, base delay, max delay, and overall timeout. But defaults should be safe for most.

[04:56] Samira El-Amin: You said “overall timeout”. We also care about connect vs read timeouts. Streaming especially.

[05:03] Ibrahim Khan: Yep. This is the other standard we’re aligning: a consistent timeout model. Under the hood, TS uses fetch + AbortController, Python uses an HTTP client with separate connect/read, Go uses net/http + context. The goal is to expose the same concept: overall request deadline, and optional connect/read where supported.

[05:23] Jared Kim: Streaming is the tricky one. Because “read timeout” can kill a stream even though it’s working.

[05:29] Ibrahim Khan: Exactly. For streaming, you generally want an idle timeout rather than a total read timeout, depending on your proxy behavior.

[05:37] Samira El-Amin: Speaking of proxies. This is our second big issue: streaming disconnects behind our corp gateway. We see partial tokens, then it drops.

[05:46] Priya Nair: And the SDK doesn’t always surface a clear error. Sometimes it’s just like “stream ended”.

[05:52] Ibrahim Khan: Yep. That’s another thing we’re fixing. We want typed streaming disconnect errors that include request_id when possible, and also surface partial output consistently.

[06:03] Jared Kim: Request ID is huge for us. Some SDK errors don’t include it.

[06:07] Ibrahim Khan: Agreed. We’re standardizing that too. The platform is also making sure request_id is present in errors consistently.

[06:15] Monica Patel: The goal is when you paste a request_id into a support ticket, we can locate the exact trace.

[06:21] Samira El-Amin: Let’s talk about streaming retries. Do you automatically retry a stream if it disconnects mid-way?

[06:29] Ibrahim Khan: Not by default, no. And that’s intentional.

[06:33] Priya Nair: Because duplicate side effects?

[06:35] Ibrahim Khan: Exactly. If you retry a generation call, you might get a different completion, or you might double-charge if you don’t dedupe. More importantly, from an app behavior standpoint, auto-retrying a partially delivered stream can be confusing.

[06:52] Jared Kim: But if it disconnects at like token 30, users get a cut off sentence. That’s also bad.

[06:58] Ibrahim Khan: Totally. So our recommended pattern is: (1) if you need safe retries, include an idempotency key where applicable, and (2) for streaming, treat disconnect as an error and decide in your app whether to retry from scratch, or fall back to non-streaming for that request, or show “regenerate”.

[07:16] Samira El-Amin: Do you support idempotency keys now?

[07:19] Monica Patel: We have guidance and we’re expanding it. Some endpoints accept idempotency headers; the consistent part is you always get a request_id back, and you can log it.

[07:30] Priya Nair: So you’re not doing “resume stream from token 31”?

[07:34] Ibrahim Khan: No, not at this time.

[07:36] Jared Kim: Okay, that’s reasonable. But then we need clarity: what does the SDK return when it disconnects? Exception? Partial text? Both?

[07:46] Ibrahim Khan: The standard we’re implementing: the iterator/stream yields chunks as normal; if it disconnects unexpectedly, the SDK raises a typed exception that includes: request_id if known, status_code if known, and a reason classification like “network_error”, “timeout”, “server_closed”. Partial text you already got is yours; we won’t swallow it.

[08:07] Samira El-Amin: But can you give us the partial in the exception too? For easier logging.

[08:11] Ibrahim Khan: We’re debating that because it can be huge and sensitive. We’re leaning towards: provide a hook to capture it, but don’t automatically attach full partial output to error objects because people log errors.

[08:26] Jared Kim: That’s good. Please don’t put prompts or outputs into logs by default.

[08:31] Monica Patel: That’s also part of our security posture. We’re careful about secret handling and redaction.

[08:38] Priya Nair: On the disconnects: what do you see commonly? Is it your side or our side?

[08:44] Ibrahim Khan: Most common is proxies timing out idle connections, or buffering issues. Another one is corporate TLS inspection boxes doing weird half-close. We’ve seen “server FIN mid-chunk” type behavior too.

[08:59] Samira El-Amin: That sounds like what we see. The gateway has an idle timeout at 60 seconds.

[09:05] Jared Kim: And our streaming sometimes pauses longer than that when the model is thinking.

[09:09] Ibrahim Khan: Yeah, so two things: (1) make sure you’re using server-sent events / chunked response and the server sends heartbeats if supported, and (2) tune timeouts so the client doesn’t kill it prematurely. On our side, we try to flush tokens regularly, but there are cases where you can get a gap.

[09:28] Priya Nair: Do you do heartbeats today?

[09:30] Ibrahim Khan: In some paths we have keep-alive behavior, but it’s not a formal “heartbeat event” across all SDKs yet. Part of the parity work is standardizing the event stream types so you can tell “token vs metadata vs end”.

[09:45] Samira El-Amin: When is that parity work landing?

[09:48] Monica Patel: We’re targeting the next set of SDK releases over the next few weeks. There’s an audit and then staged releases, with migration notes. It’s actively in-flight.

[10:00] Jared Kim: Is this going to be breaking?

[10:02] Monica Patel: Minimal breaking changes is the goal. Where behavior changes, we’ll call it out and provide flags or migration notes.

[10:09] Ibrahim Khan: For example, changing retry defaults can surprise folks, so we’ll document it and keep it conservative.

[10:17] Priya Nair: Can you share the planned defaults? Like max attempts and timeout defaults.

[10:22] Ibrahim Khan: I can share what we’re standardizing on, yes. It’s basically: retry on 429 and transient 5xx and network errors, limited attempts, exponential backoff with jitter, honor Retry-After, and a sensible overall timeout. Streaming: no automatic retries; clear errors; request_id always surfaced.

[10:44] Jared Kim: That’s directionally what we want. But I need numbers to evaluate. Like base delay 200ms vs 1s matters.

[10:52] Ibrahim Khan: Understood. I’ll send the draft standard after this call. We’ve run some internal experiments under simulated 429 and 5xx.

[11:02] Samira El-Amin: Okay, can we switch to “duplicate billing concern” for a second? If a retry happens after you already processed a request, how do we know?

[11:12] Ibrahim Khan: Great question. Without idempotency keys, you can’t guarantee dedupe across the network. What we do is: provide request_id per attempt; SDK also increments retry_count and can surface it in logs/hooks. For charges, we can help correlate by request_id.

[11:29] Monica Patel: And we strongly recommend not retrying on 4xx except 429. So you shouldn’t get duplicate “bad request” charges because we wouldn’t retry that.

[11:39] Jared Kim: But what about network timeout after server processed it? That’s the classic.

[11:43] Ibrahim Khan: Exactly. That’s why we keep attempts low and why idempotency keys are recommended for anything you might retry.

[11:51] Priya Nair: If the SDK times out, is it treated like retryable?

[11:56] Ibrahim Khan: Generally yes, timeouts are retryable, but we avoid infinite loops. And if the overall timeout is reached, we stop.

[12:07] Jared Kim: We need to ensure “overall timeout” actually works for streaming. Some clients only timeout on connect.

[12:14] Ibrahim Khan: Yup. In TS, AbortController needs to be wired correctly so it cancels the streaming reader. In Go, context cancellation must stop reading from the body. In Python, the read timeout behavior differs between libraries. These are exactly the bugs we’re cleaning up.

[12:33] Samira El-Amin: Okay so right now, is TS more reliable than Python or vice versa?

[12:38] Ibrahim Khan: It depends on the edge case. TS has had cases where it didn’t parse Retry-After formats correctly. Python had cases where streaming timeouts weren’t honored properly. Go had gaps on Retry-After handling historically. We’re aligning all three.

[12:57] Priya Nair: That’s helpful honesty.

[13:00] Monica Patel: (cross talk) Yeah.

[13:01] Jared Kim: Can we talk about classification of network errors? Like ECONNRESET, ENOTFOUND, TLS handshake.

[13:09] Ibrahim Khan: Yes. Network errors where you didn’t get an HTTP response are generally retryable with backoff, up to the attempt cap. TLS handshake failures can be transient but also misconfig; still often treated as retryable once or twice.

[13:24] Samira El-Amin: What about DNS failures?

[13:26] Ibrahim Khan: Same story. Usually retryable but if it persists, it’s your resolver. Cap keeps you safe.

[13:35] Jared Kim: Do you do any server hints besides Retry-After? Like “please don’t retry” codes.

[13:41] Ibrahim Khan: We have error codes in the response body that map to retryable vs terminal. The SDKs will classify based on status code and error code.

[13:53] Priya Nair: Are those codes stable?

[13:55] Monica Patel: They’re becoming more stable. We’re cleaning up the enum so SDKs can rely on it.

[14:02] Samira El-Amin: Okay. Streaming again: what happens if the stream disconnects but the server kept generating? Do you have any server-side cancellation?

[14:12] Ibrahim Khan: If the connection drops, the server typically notices and will stop, but there can be lag. Some runtimes keep generating until they hit the next write failure.

[14:24] Jared Kim: That’s wasted tokens.

[14:26] Ibrahim Khan: Right, but it’s generally bounded. We’re also improving detection.

[14:33] Priya Nair: In our proxy, we sometimes see buffering. Tokens arrive in bursts.

[14:38] Ibrahim Khan: Yup. That can create long idle gaps and then a burst, which triggers your idle timeout if you’re not careful.

[14:46] Samira El-Amin: So would you recommend increasing idle timeout on the gateway?

[14:49] Ibrahim Khan: Yes, if you can. Or allow websockets, but that’s a different path. For SSE/HTTP streaming, increasing idle timeouts helps.

[15:01] Monica Patel: Also, we can share what timeouts we recommend for streaming specifically.

[15:06] Jared Kim: Please do.

[15:08] Ibrahim Khan: Another thing: log request_id and also “retry_count” per request. Our SDKs will standardize those fields so you can see “attempt 1, attempt 2” etc.

[15:22] Priya Nair: Will that be in headers or in a callback?

[15:25] Ibrahim Khan: In errors, and also in a hook/callback depending on language. We’re careful with telemetry by default, but at minimum we’ll have consistent logging fields.

[15:39] Samira El-Amin: We’re very sensitive to any phone-home telemetry.

[15:43] Monica Patel: Understood. By default we’re not sending your data anywhere. It’s more about structured logging you control.

[15:52] Jared Kim: Okay. Do you have any customer examples of retry storms you’ve seen and fixed?

[16:00] Ibrahim Khan: We had an incident where during elevated 429s, some clients retried too aggressively and amplified load. That’s part of why SRE pushed for stricter defaults. It’s not fun on either side.

[16:15] Samira El-Amin: That’s exactly what we’re afraid of. We don’t want to be “that customer”.

[16:19] Monica Patel: Right.

[16:21] Priya Nair: For our app, we also do our own retry at a higher layer. How do we avoid double retries with the SDK?

[16:29] Ibrahim Khan: Great question. You should choose one layer to own retries. Our SDK allows disabling retries or setting max_attempts=1. Then you can do it in your app with your own logic.

[16:44] Jared Kim: That’s probably what we’ll do. Or at least keep SDK retries minimal.

[16:49] Samira El-Amin: Yeah we prefer explicit.

[16:52] Ibrahim Khan: Makes sense.

[16:54] Monica Patel: Can I ask: what does your traffic pattern look like? Bursty? steady? concurrency?

[17:02] Samira El-Amin: Bursty. We have user-driven spikes, plus nightly batch.

[17:06] Jared Kim: And we’re multi-tenant. One tenant can spike, then we start hitting rate limits.

[17:12] Ibrahim Khan: Then retry storms are especially dangerous. Jitter is crucial.

[17:18] Priya Nair: Do you recommend per-tenant queues?

[17:20] Monica Patel: Usually yes, but that’s more architecture. Our console has some per-route metrics, but client-side shaping is still best.

[17:31] Jared Kim: Another question: do you return 429 for both token-per-minute and requests-per-minute?

[17:36] Ibrahim Khan: Yes, and the error code can differentiate. Retry-After is intended to be meaningful in both cases, though it’s not perfect.

[17:47] Samira El-Amin: Okay. For streaming, do you ever return 429 after a stream is open?

[17:53] Ibrahim Khan: Typically 429 would happen on request start. Once streaming begins, it’s usually a network disconnect or a server error mid-flight.

[18:03] Priya Nair: We saw a mid-stream error once.

[18:06] Ibrahim Khan: That can happen if a backend crashes. In that case we want the SDK to surface a typed error with request_id.

[18:16] Jared Kim: So your platform guarantees request_id on streaming errors?

[18:20] Ibrahim Khan: The goal is yes. There are edge cases when you never got headers, then you don’t have it. But if we got headers, we will propagate it.

[18:32] Samira El-Amin: Okay. This standardization project you keep referencing—what is it exactly?

[18:38] Ibrahim Khan: It’s a cross-language SDK parity initiative: unify authentication precedence, retry/backoff, timeout models, and streaming semantics so Python/TS/Go behave the same. It includes conformance tests so we don’t regress.

[18:54] Monica Patel: It’s also driven by support volume. We’ve had too many “why does TS do X but Python does Y” tickets.

[19:03] Priya Nair: That’s reassuring.

[19:05] Jared Kim: Will you publish the standard so we can implement similarly in our internal wrappers?

[19:10] Ibrahim Khan: Yes. We’re publishing an internal standard and it’ll be reflected in docs and migration notes. I can share the current draft with you.

[19:21] Samira El-Amin: Cool.

[19:23] (brief silence)

[19:24] Monica Patel: Anything else on your mind? We can go deeper on streaming disconnect troubleshooting if you want.

[19:30] Samira El-Amin: Yeah. We have a specific symptom: behind Zscaler (or something like that), we see disconnect at around 30-40 seconds. Not always.

[19:42] Ibrahim Khan: Yep, that’s a classic. Some proxies have an idle timeout, some have a total response time limit. Also sometimes they buffer until a chunk boundary.

[19:54] Jared Kim: And our client is Node 18, fetch.

[19:57] Ibrahim Khan: Node fetch streaming works, but you must consume the stream continuously. If your code awaits too long between reads, you can trigger issues.

[20:10] Priya Nair: We use an async iterator. Sometimes we do additional processing between tokens.

[20:15] Ibrahim Khan: That can cause backpressure. Not necessarily bad, but if your processing pauses reading, proxy buffers, then you get idle timeouts.

[20:28] Samira El-Amin: Interesting. So best practice is to read fast and buffer ourselves.

[20:32] Ibrahim Khan: Exactly. Read and queue, then process from the queue.

[20:38] Jared Kim: That’s helpful.

[20:41] Monica Patel: If you send us a snippet or description we can sanity check.

[20:46] Samira El-Amin: We can share a simplified version.

[20:49] Ibrahim Khan: Great.

[20:51] Priya Nair: Does Redwood have any plans for automatic keep-alive messages in the stream?

[20:56] Ibrahim Khan: We’re evaluating. It’s tricky because it changes the event stream semantics and some clients treat it as data. But we can do structured “ping” events.

[21:10] Jared Kim: That would help proxies not kill it.

[21:12] Ibrahim Khan: Agreed.

[21:15] Monica Patel: But we don’t want to promise it today. Near term is making sure the SDK handles disconnects clearly and doesn’t mislead you.

[21:25] Samira El-Amin: Okay.

[21:27] Jared Kim: Last retry question: do you retry POST requests? Some SDKs only retry GET.

[21:33] Ibrahim Khan: We do retry POST for these inference endpoints because they are logically safe-ish, but again, idempotency is the caveat. We keep it limited and only for transient errors.

[21:48] Jared Kim: Got it.

[21:50] Priya Nair: If we disable SDK retries, do we still get Retry-After surfaced?

[21:55] Ibrahim Khan: Yes, it’ll be in the error object/headers so your wrapper can honor it.

[22:03] Samira El-Amin: Perfect.

[22:05] Monica Patel: Alright. Let’s do a quick recap and next steps.

[22:10] Monica Patel: Ibrahim will send the draft retry/timeout standard and recommended numbers. You all will send us proxy details and a couple anonymized logs for the disconnect issue. Then we’ll schedule a follow-up once you’ve reviewed. Does that work?

[22:25] Samira El-Amin: Yes.

[22:26] Jared Kim: Yep.

[22:28] Priya Nair: Sounds good.

[22:30] Ibrahim Khan: Great. And if you have any “we saw a storm at 10:03” type data, include the correlation IDs you have, even if it’s not our request_id. We can map sometimes.

[22:41] Jared Kim: Will do.

[22:43] Monica Patel: Thanks everyone.

[22:45] (call continues with light scheduling / logistics)

[23:05] Samira El-Amin: Actually one more—can you send recommended settings for batch vs interactive?

[23:10] Ibrahim Khan: Yep. I’ll include two suggested profiles.

[23:14] Monica Patel: Cool, thanks.

[23:16] End of transcript (recording ended early; remaining minutes were scheduling)
